doc.title: Victor Rendon interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 12, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Cancelling the March 2020 percussion recital and last gigs
summary: Rendón recalls his last band date at the Nuyorican on March 10, the dilemma over the college percussion recital, waiting on the dean's decision, and a final Batá ceremony on March 14.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Was there a particular day you remember, in March I’m guessing, where things started to be cancelled for you?

Most definitely. The last date that I played with my band was March 10th at the Nuyorican. It was on a Tuesday. And it hadn’t really hit anybody, at least me. I was aware that we were having a problem with the pandemic but it didn’t hit home yet. It really hit the next day, Wednesday because I had a percussion ensemble recital on the 12th and I had a group from Ireland that came in to perform with us, and I had another group from Baltimore, Maryland. And they were all here and we were ready to go. We had this big recital to present. But that’s when everything became questionable as to whether we could perform with larger groups. So the college really didn’t have an answer whether, for me to go on or not. So I was sort of like in limbo. Should I let all these people down and just cancel everything? Just go back home you know. Or go on and take a chance. So it was really something that I really had to think about. What it came down to by the evening of March 11th I decided that I was going to wait for a definite cue from the dean of the school. I just waited for the higher ups to tell me what was supposed to happen. So I got together with the person that helps me move things, and we moved the essential stuff to the room. I don’t have to do it but, you know, I always help anyway. And I said, “Well if we go on then we’ll move the small stuff in the morning, and we’re good to go.” As it happened, when I got home I had an email from the dean announcing to everybody that we couldn’t get together in large groups. So that was the final decision. But it was a tough one because it fell on me, at the beginning, on me to make a decision, and how do you make the decision? You know you’re playing with people’s lives in many ways. So it © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
was tough. But I think I did the right thing in just waiting and not just saying oh, it’s over, or we’re going to go on, you know, being hard-headed about it.

That’s interesting because you anticipated a question, because most of us musicians got quickly very used to the phone ringing or an email saying those gigs you have, they’re cancelled. But to be put in a position to cancel a gig yourself, it’s a tough one.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. And I still did, I did like actually a Batá ceremony that Saturday, and it was still not — I was aware of it and I was leery about doing it, but I just went ahead and did it anyway because it had been scheduled. And that was the last one, actually the 14th was the last function that I did. And after that we all went into quarantine and everything just got cancelled. I didn’t have to call anybody, because it was sort of understood.
